title: Apartheid: Engineering Racism in South Africa

cards.h: A system built on the law
cards.b:
Apartheid was a system of racial laws that ruled South Africa from 1948 to the early 1990s. It classed people by race, separated them in homes and schools, and denied the black majority the vote.

Apartheid is one of the clearest examples of how laws can build injustice. Its end is also one of the great stories of the 20th century.

In 1948 the National Party, led by Afrikaner nationalists, won the white vote in South Africa. It promised to keep white rule and to separate the races more firmly. The word apartheid means "apartness" in Afrikaans.

The party drew on fears about the growth of black cities and the political movements that were challenging segregation. It set out to make the system permanent through law.

cards.h: The laws that built the system
cards.b:
The Population Registration Act of 1950 sorted every South African into a racial group. The Group Areas Act of 1950 forced people to live in separate areas. The Bantu Education Act of 1953 set up a separate school system with less money for black children.

Black South Africans had to carry pass books, and many were forced into "homelands" or Bantustans, which were given a nominal independence. Millions were moved from their homes.

Mohandas Gandhi in South Africa (1893–1914)

Gandhi lived and worked in South Africa for over twenty years. He founded the Natal Indian Congress in 1894, and he developed satyagraha, or truth-force, as a tool of protest there.

The Indian community of South Africa was one of the first targets of racial laws, and Gandhi's early struggles shaped his later methods.
The system grew over four decades. Its end came after mass protest, economic pressure and a changing world.

On 21 March 1960 police fired on a crowd protesting against the pass laws at Sharpeville, south of Johannesburg. Sixty-nine people were killed, many of them shot in the back. The government banned the African National Congress and the Pan Africanist Congress.

Sharpeville shocked the world. It led to international condemnation and helped turn many countries against South Africa, and it pushed the ANC toward armed struggle.

Apartheid is sometimes compared to the segregation of the American South, or treated as a version of ordinary racial separation. The comparison is common in teaching.

Historians argue that apartheid was more than segregation. It was an attempt to engineer a racial society, with planned homelands, controlled movement and a system of laws designed to keep black South Africans without political rights. The scale of the state's control makes it unique.

In 1963 police raided a farm in Rivonia and arrested the leaders of the armed wing of the ANC, Umkhonto we Sizwe. At the trial in 1964 Nelson Mandela spoke of his willingness to die for the ideal of a free society. He was sentenced to life imprisonment and spent 27 years in prison.

Mandela's words became one of the most important statements of the anti-apartheid struggle. They also show how courage in court can shape a national story.

On 16 June 1976 students in Soweto protested against the forced use of Afrikaans in schools. Police opened fire, and the uprising spread across the country. Hundreds were killed, and many young activists fled into exile.

The uprising changed the struggle. It made a new generation of young leaders visible, and it forced the government to face the failure of its policies.

International sanctions, divestment campaigns and the boycott of South African goods grew through the 1980s. Business and government leaders inside South Africa also came to see that apartheid could not last.

Historians argue about how much each pressure mattered. The interplay of internal protest, the economy and the end of the Cold War made change possible. The end was not a single event but a long process.

Nelson Mandela was released in February 1990. Negotiations led to a new constitution, and the first democratic elections were held in April 1994. The ANC won a large majority, and Mandela became the country's first black president.

The transition was not peaceful in every place, but it avoided the civil war many had feared. The new South Africa was built on a constitution with a bill of rights.

When Gandhi returned to India in 1915, he carried his South African experience with him. Satyagraha became the core of the Indian freedom movement, and its methods inspired later struggles, including the civil rights movement in the United States and the anti-apartheid campaign.

The link runs both ways. Indian activists in South Africa worked closely with African leaders, and Indian communities were among the victims of apartheid. Two movements, two countries, one shared language of protest.

Five things to remember
  1. The National Party came to power in 1948.
  2. The Population Registration Act sorted people by race in 1950.
  3. Sharpeville (1960) and Soweto (1976) were turning points.
  4. Mandela was sentenced in 1964 and released in 1990.
  5. The first democratic elections were held in 1994.
Think about it
  • How do laws create and then destroy a system of injustice?
  • What made the end of apartheid possible?
